item.title: 'A bit strange' - Leclerc seeking outlier to catch Mercedes in Qatar
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Charles Leclerc seeking outlier as Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull try to catch Mercedes at Qatar Grand Prix

Friday 27 November 2026 20:50, UK

Charles Leclerc believes an “outlier” has given Mercedes a “massive” advantage at the Qatar Grand Prix, after Kimi Antonelli and George Russell dominated Friday’s practice sessions.

Mercedes were nearly half a second quicker than the rest of the field at the Lusail International Circuit as Antonelli topped both sessions from Russell.

Their four-tenths advantage over closest challenger Lando Norris in second practice could have been even greater, with neither Antonelli nor Russell completing a full low-fuel lap on the soft tyres. It was an ominous sign for the rest of the field ahead of Saturday's qualifying, which gets under way at 6pm, with coverage live on Sky Sports F1 from 5.15pm.

- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺

Mercedes' dominance was similar to their pace advantage earlier in the season but the second half of 2026 has largely been very close between F1's top four teams - Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren.

Ferrari were over one second behind Antonelli on a dismal Friday as Leclerc spun in second practice and Lewis Hamilton suffered an engine problem which brought his Ferrari to a halt.

"Honestly it's been a very difficult day. It's not that we didn't try on the softs, we couldn't improve our lap time on the mediums," said Leclerc.

"I lost the car and had some damage so we had to repair the car but that was the first lap of FP2 and I couldn't improve and even on the new soft later on I couldn't improve.

"A very, very difficult day. The feeling is just very difficult to get right. Not even on high fuel we were strong, so for now, it looks like a very difficult weekend but we are working hard to try and understand something.

"For some reason, Mercedes are so much faster than everybody expected, so the gaps are just a little bit strange, so there's something that's an outlier and we just need to find that."

Ferrari were not expected to be strong at the Lusail International Circuit due to the long flat out zones and high-speed corners but Leclerc suggested his team, along with McLaren and Red Bull were missing a trick that will give them more pace.

"I don't think we know yet what's the outlier. I think other teams probably didn't find that because Mercedes still have a massive advantage," he said.

"We are going to work towards that and analyse the data to understand what's going on."

Norris: Mercedes not even worth thinking about

McLaren were predicted to be very competitive in Qatar due to their strength in the high-speed corners but Norris and Piastri were never close to matching the pace of Mercedes.

On Saturday, McLaren are expected to put the new floor they ran in Las Vegas on the car but Norris does not think it will make a big enouch difference to catch Mercedes who are in "a different category".

"I don't know how much that will help around here compared to Vegas," said last year's world champion.

"But obviously tonight [Friday] we will see how much we can gain from that. It's not going to be the gap we need.

"We are probably seven tenths off the Mercedes a lap so it's not even worth thinking about them. But relative to the rest we seem to be in a good place. The fact we can have the new floor on tomorrow will add a little bit and a little bit is better than nothing. We seem in a relatively decent place."

Both Antonelli and Russell pointed out that Verstappen will always be a threat and the four-time world champion is coy about his chances of challenging the Mercedes in qualifying.

"A bit of a difficult day. The balance of the car is a bit too disconnected at the moment to go fast, so that's what we need to fix," said the Red Bull driver.

"The all-round balance is not there at the moment and is costing us quite a bit of lap time. We will keep trying and see how good we can get it."

"Mercedes look quite far ahead on the short run and long run. Let's see how much we can close the gap."

item.title: Taylor says he is quitting darts for good after comeback
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good as he and Adrian Lewis are knocked out of MODUS Super Series

Phil Taylor retired from professional darts in 2018; he came out of retirement for this week's MODUS Super Series International Pairs, teaming up with friend Adrian Lewis; the Pair finished second-bottom in group C and were knocked out of the event

Friday 27 November 2026 20:51, UK

Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good and has no plans to come out of retirement again.

The 16-time world champion was lured back to the oche for this year's MODUS Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth alongside his long-time friend Adrian Lewis.

The English duo lost all five of their matches on Thursday but rebounded on Friday, winning three and losing two matches, to finish second-bottom in the Group C standings.

- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results, schedule

- Luke Littler faces nightmare route at World Championship

- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract

Taylor, 67, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after winning his final world crown, and when asked if he would make another comeback, the 14-time PDC World Championship winner told Pluto TV: "[This is] proper retirement."

A heartwarming moment unfolded after Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-3 in their final group match against Scotland, as each of the other nations arrived to give Taylor a guard of honour, as he walked away from the oche.

"I mean I'm 67, I get my pension next February," Taylor said, when asked if this would be his last competitive appearance. "I'm a pensioner now, officially!"

"I'll still do personal appearances, more having a chat with people, talking about my career, that kind of thing."

Taylor and Lewis, who teamed up to win four World Cup of Darts titles between 2012 and 2016, finished Thursday at the bottom of Group C. Friday started poorly for the Englishmen, losing to Denmark's Ivan Springborg-Poulsen and Andreas Toft Jørgensen 4-2.

Speaking on his retirement U-turn this week, Taylor said: "I was dreading it to be honest with you because I know I wasn't playing like I can do, but now I've been here and it's all over, I've loved it."

The pair hit back on Friday with a 4-3 win against Germany, then beat Switzerland and Sweden, both 4-2.

The Englishmen would tie Scotland at three legs apiece in his final competitive match, before Taylor missed a checkout for 48 for victory, in what would have been a fairy-tale finish.

"Looking back now, it's like it never happened," Taylor said, reflecting on his glittering career.

"I've said to other people who have been on stage and retired: 'How do you feel now?'

"'It's like you've never been there'. It's ever so weird. And you come up on YouTube and you just go: "No, I know. I know I was there, but I can't remember it."

"It's very, very strange because, mentally-wise, you move on. That was your former life and now my life is different."

Instead of flying around the world competing, Taylor says retirement has allowed him to spend more time with his grandchildren.

"I've got 11 grandchildren," Taylor said. "So I spend a lot of time with them now.

"[I do] things I've never done before. Go to bed when I want; I go to bed early. For me, 9pm would be like, I'd be asleep two hours before 9pm, and it's great.

"I love getting up early as well. We can do all the chores. We can go shopping and get everything done, and it isn't even 11am. It's great!

"People say I'm the GOAT [Greatest of All Time]-I'm an old goat now!"

item.title: Campagnolo Super Record X review: Gucci gravel gearing
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Standing on the opposite side of the world, looking in, Campagnolo had seemingly had a rough few years. A lot was riding on the iconic Italian manufacturer’s new groupset lineup, consisting of 1x and 2x variations of Super Record designed to span road and gravel, each with 13 speeds in the back, wireless shifting, and hydraulic braking. Since then, Campagnolo has brought those options down a pricing tier to Record, has earned a decent amount of praise, and has taken on some outside investment.

This review looks at Super Record X (SR X), Campagnolo’s top-tier, partly Italian-made, and eye-wateringly-priced 1x-specific gravel groupset. It’s arguably the only groupset that directly competes with SRAM’s flagship RED XPLR E1, especially given that Shimano doesn’t yet have a top-tier gravel-focused option.

For those keen on a different version of the groupset, Super Record X shares plenty of tech with Campagnolo’s other 13-speed wireless options. The wholly revised shifters are shared across all Wireless 13 groups, and same goes for the brakes. Shift quality, the battery system, and general servicing are all the same, too. And all that stuff is equally applicable to the more affordable Record range.

Before we uncork this European-made groupset review, it’s worth noting that I arrived at testing Campagnolo’s latest flagship offering with scepticism. While it may be brutal to admit, I haven’t been excited to own or recommend Campagnolo components since 11-speed was considered innovative, and even then, I thought they’d made some missteps compared to the legendary 10-speed generation.

Along the way, Campagnolo not only managed to underwhelm me, but they also had products that straight up upset me. There were three generations of problematic EPS (Campagnolo’s earlier electronic shifting) that at times felt like owning a modern Alfa Romeo with the electronics on the fritz. Meanwhile, many liked Campagnolo’s entry into gravel with its Ekar 13-speed mechanical shifting, including some people whose opinions I trusted. I thought I was going crazy for thinking the ergonomics and shift quality were disappointing. So I arrived at this test thinking that if I like this stuff and it works without fault, then I damn better shout about it. So:

This stuff is good!

Highs: A high-end product throughout, where the quality is felt in the shift buttons, aesthetics, and ownership. Comfortable hoods with multiple shift options. 10-48T gear range option likely to find favour with many. Record version feels and functions the same, and is priced directly against GRX Di2 and Force XPLR.

Lows: Thumb lever placed a little too rearward for intuitive thumb levering. Shifter shape not optimised for small hands. A labyrinth of instruction manuals. Spares availability more scarce than the two S’s in many parts of the world. Price is comparatively high in the USA. Brakes feel great, but power lags behind the competition. Shortest crank length is 165 mm.

Price: Complete Super Record X groupset from €3,497 / US$4,475 / AU$5,519. Record X from €2,200 / US$2,678 / AU$3,789.

The basic rundown

Campagnolo may have upset many of its loyalists by deleting the thumb shifter in its first wireless groupset (WRL), but a short two years later, they rectified that with Super Record Wireless 13. That new shifter, shared amongst all new Super Record options, brought back one of Campagnolo’s more unique features, albeit with a modern twist.

This fully revised shifter offers a paddle behind the brake lever, a rethought “thumb” paddle on the inner side of the hood (also reachable with a wrapped-around finger), and a third button on the upper inside of the hood to be configured for shifting or accessory control. The whole hood shape has been reworked, with a flatter rear profile that doesn’t feel out of place against the latest from Shimano or SRAM, while the front section retains a signature hook.

With the introduction of SR X comes a 1x-specific left-only lever option that removes the buttons and electronic guts. This saves 20 grams and some money for those who only want to operate the gears from the right shifter. I opted for the regular left shifter, which gave plenty of options for shifting customisation, including the option to operate it SRAM-style (left hand sends the derailleur one way, right hand goes back the other way).

Wirelessly synced to those shifters are reworked derailleurs. There’s a range of 2x and 1x options, and Super Record X (SR X) has its own 1x-specific version. Where SRAM’s XPLR E1 requires a UDH-compatible frame to fit the unique Full Mount derailleur, Campagnolo has kept it traditional, mounting to whatever derailleur hanger your frame has. That SR X derailleur is reinforced for off-road use and offers a longer cage for pairing with Campagnolo’s 9-42T or 10-48T cassettes. A sprung clutch-type mechanism, the same as Ekar, provides increased chain control (although, as I’ll get to, not as much as others).

Powering the derailleur is a new removable and rechargeable battery. Packing 450 mAh, it’s bigger in capacity and physical size than SRAM’s 300 mAh unit. Campagnolo quotes 750 km of riding from a single charge, but keep in mind that nobody’s use case is identical. Charging can be done with the battery on or off the bike, using yet another proprietary USB-C magnetic charge cable (included with the battery).

First introduced with Ekar, the 13-speed cassettes continue to require Campagnolo’s own N3W freehub design, which is effectively a chopped version of its earlier freehub that allows the fitment of smaller 9T or 10T cogs. It’s a freehub design that’s well catered for by Campagnolo, sibling brand Fulcrum, DT Swiss, and quite a few other premium hub and wheel options.…

item.title: Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice

World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.

Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.

Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.

The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.

Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.

The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.

"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.

"But it was very interesting to see how the car behaved after those changes. It's not easy."

Antonelli, who secured his maiden title in Mexico City earlier this month, was also fastest in the opening session on the mediums. Mercedes did fit the 20-year-old with the soft tyre in the first hour, but he failed to set a lap time on them.

He said he feels it will be close between himself and Russell for the race victory, but added: "You can never write off Max [Verstappen] and the others."

Norris, meanwhile, said Mercedes "were in a different category" to McLaren, highlighting the Silver Arrows "were quicker in every single corner by miles".

The 2025 world champion added: "We seem in a relatively decent position, similar on pace with Red Bull, and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I'd say it's OK."

Four-time title winner Verstappen said it had been a "difficult day" following his issues with heavy steering towards the end of the session.

"The balance of the car is probably too disconnected at the moment to go fast," he added. "It's costing us quite a bit of lap time."

1 of 5

Hamilton also had a moment with Verstappen that was noted by the race control. The Briton was on a flying lap when he got too close to the Dutchman, who was on a long run.

Verstappen said Hamilton had moved under braking, but the stewards decided no further investigation was needed.

The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was sixth on the timesheets, with Leclerc leading Hamilton in seventh and eighth, 1.3 seconds away from Antonelli's time.

The two Racing Bulls of British rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were ninth and 10th.

Leclerc had to head back into the garage after spinning and going through the gravel when Lawson was just ahead of him at Turn Nine.

The Monegasque driver said the car did not feel right, and the Italian team spent a chunk of time repairing the damage to the floor. After the session he said he lost control after going a little bit early on the throttle.

Ferrari arrived in Qatar after another on-track incident between Leclerc and Hamilton, this time in Las Vegas. The pair made contact and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, with Hamilton saying on Thursday the team were facing "very, very challenging times".

Leclerc thinks this weekend could potentially be another struggle for the Italian team, who can secure second in the constructors' championship if they can retain at least a 44-point lead over third-placed Red Bull.

"A very, very difficult day. Not even on high fuel were we strong," said Leclerc.

"We are working hard but for some reason, Mercedes is so much faster than I think everyone expected. So the gaps are just a little bit strange."

Drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at the Lusail circuit, meaning teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix on Sunday, which starts at 16:00 GMT.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed, 16-corner track. Laps to the grid, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

Hamilton was told by his engineer in first practice tyre degradation was "much higher than expected" after highlighting his own issues.

Qatar and next week's finale in Abu Dhabi are going ahead as planned despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.

item.title: Wales aim to finish historic campaign with Japan win
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Wales aim to finish historic campaign with Japan win

It is not the traditional ending to a Wales rugby autumn campaign.

After the euphoria and then disappointment of two epic international weekends in Cardiff, Wales face the prospect of finishing a November series in south west London with a fixture against Japan.

It sounds unusual because the conclusion of the inaugural Nations Championship is exactly that.

The concept of a finals weekend in one venue with six games over three days is laudable, but trying to get Welsh fans excited about defeating Japan to finish ninth rather than 10th in a 12-team tournament at a neutral ground is a tough sell, especially when you compare it to what happened in Cardiff two weeks ago.

This autumn will always be remembered as the campaign where Wales shocked the rugby world by beating New Zealand for the first time since 1953.

Either side of that momentous day, there has been a lacklustre 28-21 defeat of Japan and a narrow 29-26 loss against Australia in a game Wales could and maybe should have won.

Those exciting occasions in Cardiff will now be followed by a trip to Twickenham to take on Eddie Jones' Japan. It takes some getting used to.

Wales v Japan

Nations Championship

Saturday, 28 November (13:10 GMT)

Allianz Stadium, Twickenham

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra 2 on BBC Sounds

Wales face double-header dilemma

It will be a strange experience with Wales facing Japan on a Saturday afternoon before England play New Zealand for third place.

Is it a double-header or will Wales be providing the curtain-raiser to the main event?

Whichever way you view the occasion, Wales head coach Steve Tandy knows his side will have to provide their own atmosphere with a sparse crowd present for Friday afternoon's match between Italy and Fiji before Ireland took on Australia in the evening.

"We've spoken about it all week," said Tandy.

"There's also a 40-minute bus trip which is not normal either because we usually stay closer.

"We have also spoken about it being an early kick-off.

"There might be people walking in while the game is going on, the crowd might fill up as the game goes on, so there's all these little things to consider.â

Tandy says the squad know Twickenham will not match the intensity of Cardiff's Principality Stadium during the past couple of weeks.

"It is a different type of atmosphere for us after three massive games at home and being unbelievably well supported," said Tandy.

"We've got to adapt a different sort of mindset and create that energy on the field for ourselves."

- Jenkins ready to resume Wales captaincy role

- A world-class winger - Louis Rees-Zammit 2.0

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere table of the inaugural Nations Championship to face Japan, who finished in the same position in the southern standings.

It will be the fifth time in 16 months the two sides have faced each other, with Wales winning three out of the four games.

So opposing coaches Tandy and Jones will again lock horns.

"I am looking forward to seeing him once more but it is probably a little bit too much," said Tandy, who saw his side labour to an 28-21 win over Japan three weeks ago.

Since that result, Japan have suffered a 78-15 hammering by England and a 67-5 drubbing by Scotland.

"We can't be fooled by the scoreboards, Japan have still got the core of their forward pack and line-out pressure," said Tandy.

"We're going to have to produce one of our best performances of the tournament to make sure we finish the campaign the way we want to."

Japan are down to their bare bones after a hard programme they are not used to, but Jones remains bullish.

"It should be good, a great occasion," said Jones.

"Wales don't like coming to Twickenham and for us, it's a great experience, so we will give it a red-hot crack."

Fighting words, but this is a chance for Wales to produce the type of commanding performance and victory that has been missing against this opposition.

Wales' three victories in the past four games against Japan have been by nine, seven and one point.

Given Tandy's selection this week and Japan's exertions in recent weeks, a commanding win should be on the agenda to match Scotland and Englandâs exploits against the Brave Blossoms.
